name: Palacio de la Isla, Burgos (Franco HQ)
text: Burgos was the political capital of Nationalist Spain: the Junta de Defensa Nacional sat here from July 1936, and on 1 October 1936 Franco was invested as head of state at the city's Capitanía General. From August 1937 until October 1939 this early-20th-century mansion on the Paseo de la Isla served as his residence and headquarters. His first government was formed in Burgos in January 1938, and here on 1 April 1939 he signed the final war communiqué: 'the war has ended'. The palace now houses the Instituto Castellano y Leonés de la Lengua.
look: A neo-Renaissance mansion set in gardens on the Paseo de la Isla, west of the old town, beside the Arlanzón riverside walk.
plan: Exterior and gardens from the street; interior only during Instituto events or exhibitions. 15 minutes' walk from the cathedral; combine with the Capitanía General building on Plaza de Alonso Martínez.

name: Palacio Episcopal, Salamanca (Franco HQ 1936–37)
text: After his investiture as head of state, Franco moved his headquarters to Salamanca, installing himself in the bishop's palace beside the cathedrals, lent by Bishop Enrique Pla y Deniel — whose 1936 pastoral 'Las dos ciudades' framed the war as a crusade. From here Franco directed the attack on Madrid, the war in the North and the unification of Falange and Carlists (April 1937). German and Italian envoys and the press office operated nearby, making Salamanca the rebel zone's working capital until the move to Burgos. In October 1936 the nearby University hall saw Unamuno's famous clash with General Millán-Astray.
look: The palace facade on Plaza Juan XXIII next to the New Cathedral; since 2023 it houses the Museo Diocesano (Fernando Gallego paintings and sacred art).
plan: Museum opening hours and ticket apply; exterior free. Easily combined with the Centro Documental de la Memoria Histórica five minutes away.

name: Centro Documental de la Memoria Histórica, Salamanca
coord_source: https://www.cultura.gob.es/cultura/areas/archivos/mc/archivos/cdmh/presentacion/sedes.html (address Calle Gibraltar 2; point placed from address, not a published coordinate)
text: In 1937–38 the Nationalists set up a documents office in Salamanca to gather papers seized from Republican parties, unions, Masonic lodges and individuals — raw material for the repression, especially under the 1940 Law for the Repression of Freemasonry and Communism. The archive later became the General Archive of the Civil War, and in 2007 the Centro Documental de la Memoria Histórica. Its holdings now serve historians and relatives of victims of both sides. Catalan government papers held here were returned to Catalonia from 2006 after a long political dispute (the 'papeles de Salamanca').
look: A permanent exhibition including a reconstructed Masonic lodge room made from confiscated regalia and material on the documentation service; reading room for researchers.
plan: Exhibition free, usually weekday mornings and some afternoons — check the Ministry of Culture site; photo ID required for the reading room.
disputed: The return of the 'Salamanca papers' to Catalonia was politically contested in Salamanca and in court.

name: Monumento a los Caídos, Pamplona
text: Pamplona was the base of Gen. Emilio Mola, 'the Director' of the July 1936 coup, and Navarre sent thousands of Carlist requetés to the Nationalist side, while more than 3,000 Navarrese left-wingers were killed in the rearguard. The domed Monument to the Fallen of Navarre (Yárnoz and Eusa, 1942) honoured the Nationalist dead; from 1961 its crypt held Mola and Sanjurjo. Their remains were exhumed in 2016 and the square renamed Plaza de la Libertad. The city now plans to turn it into an interpretation centre for democratic memory, while some groups call for demolition — one of Spain's liveliest 'uncomfortable heritage' debates.
look: The massive domed building dominating the end of Avenida Carlos III, with Francoist inscriptions covered; interior murals of the 'crusade' in the dome.
plan: Exterior any time. Interior opens only for occasional exhibitions while the transformation project is under way — check the Ayuntamiento de Pamplona website.
disputed: Its future (resignification vs. demolition) remains contested among city parties and memory associations.

name: Fuerte de San Cristóbal (Alfonso XII), Ezkaba
text: This 19th-century fort on the summit of Mount Ezkaba, above Pamplona, was used as a political prison in which about 2,500 Republican prisoners from across Spain were held in damp, overcrowded casemates. On 22 May 1938 prisoners overpowered guards and some 795 escaped in the largest prison break of the war. Without maps or support they were hunted down in the hills of Navarre: around 200 were killed, most of the rest recaptured, 14 later executed after court martial, and only three reached France. Scores more died of disease in the fort; many lie in the nearby 'bottle cemetery', where names were placed in bottles on the graves.
look: Huge moats, walls and casemate galleries on the summit; 360 m to the southeast the Cementerio de las botellas with memorial markers; road and hiking routes from Ansoáin, Artika and Berriozar.
plan: Walk or drive up (road closed to traffic at times); the fort interior is closed except on organised guided visits by the Navarre government/memory groups — check dates in advance. Allow 2 hours including the cemetery.
disputed: Escape figures vary slightly between sources (795 escaped; 206–211 killed; 3 reaching France); cited from memory-association and historical literature, not re-verified here against a primary source.

name: Parque de la Memoria, Sartaguda
text: Navarre never saw front-line fighting, yet the rearguard repression of 1936 was severe. In the small Ribera village of Sartaguda at least 86 people were killed, including the socialist mayor and councillors; 45 men were shot between 2 and 4 October after being called up as 'volunteers'. It became known as 'el pueblo de las viudas', the village of widows. The Parque de la Memoria, opened in 2008 with support across most parties, is Navarre's main memorial to the victims of Francoist repression: a 7-metre wall bears the names of 3,431 Navarrese killed in their villages, at Ezkaba, in Mauthausen or in forced labour.
look: A 6,000 m² landscaped park with the long wall of names, sculptures by Basque artists and plaques.
plan: Open-air, free, any time; on the edge of the village near the swimming pools.
disputed: Total figures for Navarre's repression (commonly over 3,000) come from memory-association research; exact numbers vary.

name: Miranda de Ebro concentration camp
text: Opened in 1937 beside the railway junction, Miranda de Ebro was the longest-running of Franco's concentration camps, closing only in January 1947. Around 65,000 Republican prisoners passed through it during and after the war, including captured International Brigaders. During the Second World War it became the main internment camp for foreigners crossing the Pyrenees — escaped Allied servicemen, Poles, Belgians, Czechs, French evaders and Jewish refugees — with over 3,500 held at once in a camp built for 1,500.
look: A few remains (water tank, sections of wall, washroom ruins, a guard post) and a plaque on the old site, now among industrial plants; an interpretation centre with a reconstructed barrack and prisoner files in the town's civic centre, plus memorials in Parque Alcalde Emiliano Bajo.
plan: Old camp site visible from the road; check opening hours of the interpretation centre with Miranda's tourist office.
disputed: Total prisoner numbers are estimates. The Mapcarta/Wikidata point may mark the general camp site rather than the surviving remains or the interpretation centre.

name: San Pedro de Cardeña monastery (International Brigades camp)
text: The ancient monastery near Burgos, traditionally linked to El Cid, was turned into a concentration camp where most captured International Brigaders were held from 1938, alongside Spanish prisoners. British, Irish, American and other volunteers taken at Jarama, Belchite, Calaceite and Gandesa passed through; some were exchanged, others transferred to prisons. Army psychiatrist Antonio Vallejo-Nágera carried out pseudo-scientific studies on inmates here aiming to identify a 'Marxist' psychological type. Memoirs by former prisoners describe hunger, beatings and forced saluting.
look: The restored monastery church and cloister, today home to a Cistercian (Trappist) community; there is no major memorial to the prisoners.
plan: 10 km southeast of Burgos; the church and some areas can be visited outside services — check monastery hours. Please be discreet: it is an active monastery.
disputed: Prisoner numbers and dates of operation vary between sources; details here are from general historiography and could not be re-checked against an online source in this pass.

name: Convento de San Marcos, León (concentration camp)
text: León fell to the rebels in the first days of the war, and the vast Renaissance monastery of San Marcos was turned into one of the largest prison camps in Spain. Thousands of men — and women in a separate section — from León, Asturias and the Northern front were crowded into its halls and stables, with many taken out for execution or dying of disease. The same building had been a pilgrim hospital on the Camino de Santiago; today it is a luxury Parador, and survivors' associations have long pressed for proper recognition of its prison past.
look: The famous Plateresque façade on the Bernesga river, the church and cloister (museum); the hotel interior is not a memorial site.
plan: Façade free; church/museum with small fee (check hours). Be aware the building's prison history is barely signposted.
disputed: Estimates of prisoner numbers (often cited as up to 7,000 at a time) and deaths vary and were not re-verified in this pass.

name: Valdenoceda prison memorial
text: In an old silk factory in the Valdivielso valley north of Burgos, the Franco regime ran a prison for Republican prisoners, many transferred from other jails and from the Northern front. Cold, hunger and disease killed well over a hundred inmates, who were buried in the village cemetery. In the 2000s the association Pozo de Valdenoceda exhumed and identified many of them, making it one of the best-documented cases of prison mortality in Franco's Spain.
look: The shell of the factory-prison beside the Ebro, and the cemetery with memorial for the prisoners.
plan: Small village on the N-232 about 1 h from Burgos; building exterior only; cemetery accessible.
disputed: Figures here (well over a hundred deaths, often cited as 154) are from general memory literature and were not re-verified in this pass.

name: Isla de San Simón (concentration camp), Ría de Vigo
text: Galicia fell to the coup within days in July 1936, and the rearguard repression was severe. The small island of San Simón, a former lazaretto in the Ría de Vigo, became a concentration camp and penal colony for political prisoners — first from Vigo and Pontevedra, later from across Spain, including many older prisoners. Overcrowding, hunger and disease killed hundreds (around 250 in 1941 alone), and some inmates were taken out and shot. Declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1999, the island is now a cultural centre dedicated partly to memory.
look: The restored island buildings, bridge to San Antón islet, and memorial and literary route; guided tours explain the camp period.
plan: Reached only by boat on organised visits (free guided trips by catamaran from Cesantes or Chapela, seasonal, book ahead); about 2 hours.

name: La Granja offensive battlefield (Cabeza Grande, Matabueyes)
text: To relieve pressure on Bilbao, the Republic launched an attack across the Sierra de Guadarrama towards Segovia. General Walter's 35th Division, including the XIV International Brigade, struck from the Navacerrada pass on 30 May 1937 against Nationalist positions on the heights of Cabeza Grande and Matabueyes above La Granja. Initial gains were lost to counter-attacks and Condor Legion air strikes; the offensive was called off within a week with heavy Republican losses. Hemingway set 'For Whom the Bell Tolls' against the preparations for this attack.
look: Mountain slopes and pine forest between the CL-601 (Puerto de Navacerrada road) and La Granja; scattered trenches and positions remain in the forest.
plan: Coordinates are La Granja town only — the positions lie in the hills to the south; hike with a map/local guide. Avoid duplicating the Madrid-side Guadarrama stops.
town: Real Sitio de San Ildefonso (La Granja)
disputed: Exact positions of Cabeza Grande and Matabueyes and surviving remains could not be verified online in this pass; casualty figures vary.

name: La Barranca cemetery memorial, Lardero (La Rioja)
text: La Rioja, like Navarre, fell to the rebels without a fight in July 1936, yet around two thousand people were killed in the rearguard repression in the following months. La Barranca, on the outskirts of Lardero near Logroño, was one of the main execution and burial sites: some 400 people are believed to have been shot and buried here. Relatives' association La Barranca turned the site into a memorial cemetery; it is the principal place of remembrance for the victims of repression in La Rioja.
look: A small walled memorial cemetery with name plaques and flowers left by relatives.
plan: Outside Lardero, a short drive from Logroño; free, open air. Coordinates are Lardero town centre — site location to be confirmed.
disputed: Victim numbers for La Barranca and for La Rioja as a whole are estimates from memory associations; not re-verified in this pass.
